title: Source A - diary extract (fictional practice source written by the student's teacher)
text:
Extract from the private diary of Hans-Georg Lindemann, a junior official in the German Foreign Office in Berlin, entry dated Monday 9 March 1936. [Fictional practice source: Lindemann is an invented person and this diary does not exist.]

Two days have passed since our battalions crossed the Rhine bridges at Cologne and Mainz, and still the French have not moved. Neurath told us this morning that Paris will appeal to the League and go to London rather than to the frontier. The Führer, I am told, did not sleep on Saturday night; Blomberg wanted the men back on the east bank the moment a single French division stirred. In the Ministry the joke is that Locarno died in its own bed and nobody sent flowers. The British are the key. Their ambassador said only that the matter must go to the League, and one of their lords is reported to have said that we have merely walked into our own back garden. Nineteen thousand soldiers and some police: that is the whole of our 'invasion', and yet the Paris papers write of a hundred thousand. Let them. The Führer told Neurath that had the French marched we should have had to retreat with our tails between our legs. But they will not march. Their elections come in April, and no Frenchman will die for a treaty his own government has already half abandoned.
